uncited: **Inputs:** A scalar field $f(x)$ (or $f(x,y,z)$) and an exponent parameter $p$.
The method operates on the scalar values of the volume data.
No additional complex structures are required beyond the input volume and the computed gradient magnitude.
**Calculate Gradient Magnitude:** Compute the absolute value of the derivative of the input signal.
**Raise to Power:** Raise the gradient magnitude to the exponent $p$ to accentuate regions of rapid change.
**Modulate Intensity:** Multiply the original input signal by the raised gradient result.
Higher powers narrow the highlight and introduce more high frequencies, creating a more mirror-like appearance.
*   **Aliasing:** The gradient operator acts as a high-pass filter (Fourier transform $j\omega$), damping low frequencies and enhancing high frequencies.
Raising the gradient to a power further increases these high frequencies.
*   **Performance:** Adding Phong lighting with on-the-fly gradient calculation increases computational cost compared to simple raycasting.
The technique is based on Phong shading [Phong 75], a common technique in volume rendering to give users more three-dimensional shape cues [Levoy 88].
